title: The mathematics in middle-aged Arab caliphate and it application to contemporary teaching in high schools
extended_summary:
This paper surveys major mathematical contributions of scholars from the medieval Arab caliphate and argues that this historical material can be used to stimulate students’ interest and mutual respect in contemporary mathematics teaching. Rather than evaluating a new instructional technology or intervention, the article presents historical and mathematical exposition centered on the development of algebra, number theory, trigonometry, and related topics in Islamic civilization.

The paper discusses a series of classical mathematical puzzles and then summarizes the work of figures such as al-Khwarizmi, Thabit ibn Qurra, al-Haytham, al-Karaji, Ibn Tahir al-Baghdadi, Omar Khayyam, al-Samawal, al-Tusi, and al-Qalasadi. These contributions are framed as content that can be incorporated into high school mathematics lessons, especially to enrich algebra and mathematical history teaching.

The context is contemporary high school mathematics education, but the paper does not report an empirical classroom study, participant sample, or measured achievement outcomes. Its main conclusion is that Arabic and Islamic mathematical heritage is rich and pedagogically useful as cultural and historical material for secondary mathematics instruction.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a historical review/opinion-style article rather than an empirical study. It reports no research design, no participant sample, and no measured outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides no evidence of measurable educational impact and no intervention effects. Its contribution is descriptive and curricular, not evaluative.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not evaluate any instructional technology, AI system, or student learning intervention. It is a historical/expository article describing Arab mathematicians and suggesting that some problems and historical content could be used in high school teaching. No achievement data, sample, control group, or effect estimates are reported.
